maths_eduqas_h.1.19.summary: Iteration is a powerful numerical method used to approximate solutions to equations that cannot be solved algebraically by standard rearrangement or factorisation. By rearranging an equation into the standard form x_{n+1} = f(x_n), a starting guess x_0 is repeatedly substituted into the iterative formula to generate a sequence of increasingly accurate approximations. Mastering this topic requires complete understanding of recursive sequences, convergence, divergence, and interpreting the output values against sign-change proof principles.

core.p: When algebraic methods fail to solve complex non-linear equations, mathematicians use numerical iteration to home in on the exact root. The process works by taking an initial guess and feeding it recursively through a rule until the numbers stabilise to the required degree of accuracy.
bullets: Used for equations containing mixed algebraic and transcendental terms
Replaces exact solutions with high-precision decimal approximations
Relies on rearranging a given equation into a step-by-step formula
Generates a sequence of values denoted by x_0, x_1, x_2, etc.

callouts.p: An equation written in the form x_{n+1} = f(x_n) which allows the next term in a sequence to be calculated directly from the current term.
The final converged value represents an approximate root of the original equation f(x) = 0.

fig.cap: Visualising how iteration steps bounce or staircase towards the root intersection point.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="0" y="0" width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc" rx="8"/><line x1="50" y1="200" x2="350" y2="200" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="80" y1="220" x2="80" y2="40" stroke="#334155" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M 100 180 Q 200 40 320 60" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="80" y1="200" x2="340" y2="60" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-dasharray="4,4" stroke-width="1.5"/><circle cx="140" cy="145" r="4" fill="#16a34a"/><text x="145" y="140" font-size="11" fill="#16a34a">x1</text><circle cx="210" cy="105" r="4" fill="#16a34a"/><text x="215" y="100" font-size="11" fill="#16a34a">x2</text><text x="200" y="225" font-size="11" fill="#334155">x axis</text></svg>

core.p: To perform iteration, you must first manipulate the given equation into a form where x is isolated on the left-hand side. There are often multiple ways to rearrange a single equation, but only certain arrangements will successfully converge to the root.
bullets: Start with an equation set to zero: f(x) = 0
Manipulate algebraically to isolate one x term: x = g(x)
Add subscript indices to convert into an iterative formula: x_{n+1} = g(x_n)
Check that the chosen rearrangement satisfies convergence criteria

callouts.p: If an iterative formula diverges away from the root, you must choose a different algebraic rearrangement of the same equation.

core.p: Subscript notation is vital for keeping track of the recursive steps in an iterative sequence. Understanding what each index represents prevents catastrophic errors in exam questions.
bullets: x_0 is always the starting value or initial guess provided in the question
x_1 is the first calculated approximation using x_0
x_n represents the current term in the sequence
x_{n+1} represents the next term to be calculated

callouts.p: The subscript tells you the position of the term in the sequence, not an algebraic power.

core.p: Examiners award method marks for showing clear substitution values, but using calculator memory features ensures maximum accuracy and prevents rounding errors accumulating mid-calculation.
bullets: Type your initial guess x_0 into the calculator and press equals (=)
Input the iterative formula using the Ans key for x_n
Press equals repeatedly to generate x_1, x_2, x_3, etc.
Write down every generated value to at least 4 decimal places unless instructed otherwise

callouts.p: Using the Ans button avoids retyping long decimals and speeds up iterative calculations in Component 2.

core.h: 5. Connecting Iteration to Proof by Sign Change
core.p: Iteration is intimately linked with locating roots between two integers using interval bisection and sign change principles. Before starting an iteration, you must verify that a root exists in that region.
bullets: Evaluate the function f(x) at two integer values a and b
If f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs (one positive, one negative), a root lies between them
Choose your initial guess x_0 from somewhere inside this interval [a, b]
Ensures your iteration homes in on the correct local root

callouts.p: If f(a) < 0 and f(b) > 0, continuous function f(x) must have at least one real root between a and b.

core.p: Not all iterative formulas work. Depending on the steepness of the gradient at the root, the generated sequence will either march steadily towards the solution or violently fly away from it.
bullets: Convergence occurs when successive approximations get closer and closer to the exact root
Divergence occurs when successive approximations grow larger or oscillate wildly away from the root
Mathematically, convergence requires the absolute gradient of the rearrangement function to be less than 1 near the root: |g'(x)| < 1
Exam questions will always provide a working rearrangement that converges safely

callouts.p: If your values start alternating between wildly positive and negative numbers, your iteration is diverging.

core.p: Examiners demand clear, structured presentation of iterative calculations. Simply writing down the final answer will score zero marks; every intermediate decimal must be visible.
bullets: State the starting value x_0 clearly at the top
Show the substitution calculation for x_1: x_1 = f(x_0)
List each subsequent term clearly with its index: x_2 = ..., x_3 = ...
Continue generating values until two consecutive terms match to the required degree of accuracy

callouts.p: Setting out your working in a neat list or small table prevents transposition errors during high-pressure exams.

core.p: Knowing when to stop iterating is a core skill tested at grade 9. You must continue the process until the values stabilize to the precision requested by the examiner.
bullets: Look for the instruction 'give your answer to n decimal places'
Continue calculating until x_n and x_{n+1} round to the exact same decimal value
State clearly which two terms confirm the final rounded answer
Always write the final rounded root explicitly as your conclusion

callouts.p: Stop when x_n = x_{n+1} to the specified rounding accuracy, then state that value as the root.

core.p: Before performing an iteration, exam questions often ask you to prove a root lies between two consecutive integers. This ties algebraic proofs and numerical methods together.
bullets: Substitute integer x into the original function f(x) = 0
Find one integer where f(x) is negative and the next integer where f(x) is positive
State 'change of sign, therefore root lies between x and x+1'
Use one of these integers as your initial guess x_0 for the iteration part

callouts.p: Mentioning that the function is continuous is required for top marks in rigorous sign-change proof questions.

core.p: Examiners sometimes test your ability to rearrange an equation into the requested iterative form before you can begin calculating numerical values.
bullets: Isolate the 'x' with the lowest power or inside a complex term
Factor out an x if multiple x terms appear across the expression
Divide through by coefficients to leave a clean recursive formula
Verify your rearrangement matches the format given in the proof part of the question

callouts.p: Ensure you isolate the correct x as specified in the exam paper's printed iterative formula part (a).

core.h: 11. Working with Non-Algebraic Functions in Iteration
core.p: Higher tier Eduqas papers feature iteration involving trigonometric, exponential, and logarithmic functions as well as polynomials.
bullets: Ensure your calculator is in RADIANS mode if trigonometric functions (sin, cos, tan) are involved
Handle exponential terms (e^x or a^x) with precise calculator brackets
Treat logarithmic terms using standard log laws before rearranging
Apply exact same recursive stopping rules as polynomial iterations

callouts.p: Double check whether trig questions require degrees or radians before typing your first value.

core.h: 12. Proving Accuracy to Given Decimal Places
core.p: To prove a root is correct to a specific number of decimal places (e.g. 2 decimal places), candidates must test interval bounds around that rounded value.
bullets: If testing if root is 3.45 to 2dp, test bounds at 3.445 and 3.455
Substitute these bounds into the original function f(x) = 0
Look for a change of sign between the lower and upper bounds
Conclude that since there is a sign change, the root must round to 3.45 to 2dp

callouts.p: Test values exactly halfway between rounded thresholds (e.g. for 1dp, test .05; for 2dp, test .005).

analogy.p: Imagine programming a self-guiding rocket to hit a distant target. Your initial launch coordinate is your starting guess x_0. The onboard computer measures the current distance and applies a correction formula to calculate the next position x_1. Each time the rocket fires its thrusters, it gets closer to the target (converging). If the formula was written backwards, every adjustment would blast the rocket further into deep space (diverging). Where the adjustments become so tiny that the rocket stops moving, it has found the exact target coordinate.

terms.d: A recursive numerical procedure of repeating a calculation procedure to generate a converging sequence of approximations.
An algebraic expression of the form x_{n+1} = f(x_n) used to generate successive approximations of a root.
The starting value x_0 fed into an iterative formula to begin the sequence.
The property where successive terms in an iterative sequence get progressively closer to a limiting exact root.
The property where successive terms in an iterative sequence move further away from the target root.
Indices attached to variables (e.g. x_n, x_{n+1}) indicating the position of a term within a recursive sequence.
A solution to an equation where f(x) = 0, represented graphically by an x-axis intercept.
A method of proving a root exists between two values where the function evaluates to opposite signs.
A root-finding method that repeatedly halves an interval containing a sign change.
A value where g(x) = x, representing the limit of an iterative sequence.
The required precision specified for rounding final answers, such as decimal places or significant figures.
A sequence where each term is defined as a function of the preceding term.

mistakes.w: Rounding intermediate values too early in calculations
mistakes.r: Keep full calculator precision on your screen/memory and only round the final stated answer.

mistakes.w: Writing x_1 as an algebraic power instead of an index position
mistakes.r: Understand subscripts denote sequence position, not powers or exponents.

mistakes.w: Stopping iteration after calculating only x_1
mistakes.r: Continue generating terms until two consecutive terms match to the required decimal places.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to state the initial guess x_0 in working
mistakes.r: Always explicitly state your starting value before listing x_1, x_2, etc.

mistakes.w: Using degrees instead of radians in trig iteration questions
mistakes.r: Check calculator settings immediately if trigonometric functions are present in the iteration.

mistakes.w: Confusing the original equation f(x) = 0 with the iterative rearrangement x = g(x)
mistakes.r: Ensure you substitute into the correct recursive formula provided or derived.

mistakes.w: Stating the final answer without mentioning which two terms agree
mistakes.r: Explicitly write out the matching values, e.g. x_4 = 2.345 and x_5 = 2.345, so x = 2.345.

exam.q: Show that the equation x^3 - 4x - 1 = 0 can be rearranged into the iterative formula x_{n+1} = cube_root(4x_n + 1).
model: Add 4x and 1 to both sides: x^3 = 4x + 1
Take cube root of both sides: x = cube_root(4x + 1)
Replace x with x_{n+1} and x_n to get required formula
exam.tip: Work backwards from the target formula if stuck, showing each inverse operation clearly.

exam.q: Using the iterative formula x_{n+1} = cube_root(4x_n + 1) with x_0 = 2, find x_1, x_2 and x_3. Give your answers to 4 decimal places.
model: All three values correctly stated with intermediate working shown
exam.tip: Never clear your calculator screen; use the Ans button to maintain full decimal accuracy.

exam.q: The equation x^3 - 4x - 1 = 0 has a root between x = 2 and x = 3. Perform two iterations starting with x_0 = 2 to find an estimate for this root.
exam.tip: Ensure your initial guess matches the interval specified in the question stem.

exam.q: Explain how you can prove that the root of x^3 - 4x - 1 = 0 is 2.09 correct to 2 decimal places.
model: Test bounds at half-way thresholds: evaluate f(2.085) and f(2.095)
State change of sign confirms root is 2.09 to 2 decimal places
exam.tip: Always test the boundary values (±0.005 for 2dp) in the original function f(x) = 0, not the iterative formula.

exam.q: A student uses the formula x_{n+1} = 4 / x_n + 1 to solve an equation. Explain why their iteration diverges if x_0 = 0.5.
model: Values rapidly grow larger and fail to approach a limit
State that formula diverges because successive terms move away from the root
Reference absolute gradient condition |g'(x)| >= 1 if applicable
exam.tip: Division by numbers close to zero causes values to explode rapidly.

exam.q: Rearrange x^2 + 5x - 3 = 0 into the form x = (3 - x^2) / 5. Starting with x_0 = 0.5, find x_3 to 3 decimal places.
exam.tip: Check whether the question asks for x_3 or values rounded to a specific decimal place at each step.

exam.q: Prove algebraically that x^3 - 3x - 1 = 0 has a root between x = 1 and x = 2.
model: State change of sign indicates root exists between 1 and 2 for continuous function
exam.tip: Writing out the function evaluation clearly is essential for method marks.

exam.q: Using x_0 = 1.8, apply the iterative formula x_{n+1} = (3x_n + 1)^(1/3) to find the root of x^3 - 3x - 1 = 0 to 3 decimal places. Show all your working.
model: x_4 = 1.887 (values stabilise to 1.89 or 1.88 depending on rounding; check agreement)
exam.tip: Continue until x_n and x_{n+1} match to the requested precision.

exam.q: Explain what happens if an iterative formula has a fixed point where g(x) = x.
model: State that successive iterations will produce the exact same value
The sequence has converged completely to the root
No further changes occur because x_{n+1} equals x_n
exam.tip: A fixed point represents the exact intersection of y = x and y = g(x).

exam.q: The equation x^3 + x = 7 is solved using iteration. Write down an iterative formula in the form x_{n+1} = ...
model: Rearrange x^3 + x = 7 to isolate x: x = 7 - x^3 OR x = 7 / (x^2 + 1)
Convert into iterative notation: x_{n+1} = 7 - x_n^3 (or alternative valid rearrangement)
exam.tip: More than one rearrangement is usually possible; pick the simplest one unless specified.

exam.q: A student calculates x_1 = 2.45, x_2 = 2.449, x_3 = 2.449. Write down the root to 2 decimal places and justify your answer.
model: Justification: x_2 and x_3 both round to 2.45 to 2 decimal places
exam.tip: Always explicitly link your stated root to the agreement of consecutive terms.

worked.q: Starting with x_0 = 1, use the iterative formula x_{n+1} = sqrt(5 - x_n) to find x_3. Give your answer to 3 decimal places.
steps: Write down the starting value: x_0 = 1.
Calculate x_1 by substituting x_0 into the formula: x_1 = sqrt(5 - 1) = sqrt(4) = 2.000.
Calculate x_2 using x_1: x_2 = sqrt(5 - 2) = sqrt(3) = 1.73205...
Round the final value to 3 decimal places as requested.

worked.q: Find a root of the equation x^3 - 3x - 3 = 0. Use the iterative formula x_{n+1} = cube_root(3x_n + 3) with x_0 = 2. Find x_1, x_2, and x_3 to 4 decimal places.
steps: State the initial guess: x_0 = 2.0000
Calculate x_1 = cube_root(3(2) + 3) = cube_root(9) = 2.0801
List all calculated values clearly with indices.

maths_eduqas_h.1.1.summary: Substitution is the fundamental algebraic process of replacing variables (letters) with specific numerical values to evaluate expressions or formulae. At the Higher tier, this requires mastery of the order of operations (BIDMAS/BODMAS), particularly when dealing with negative numbers, indices, and complex scientific formulae. Success in this topic bridges the gap between abstract algebraic manipulation and real-world calculation, forming the basis for solving equations and interpreting physical laws in science.

core.p: Substitution involves 'swapping' a letter for a number. Once the swap is made, the expression becomes a purely numerical calculation. It is the first step in evaluating any mathematical model.
bullets: Identify the variables in the formula or expression.
Replace every instance of the variable with the given numerical value.
Use **brackets** around the substituted number to preserve the correct sign and operation.
Perform the calculation following the strict order of operations.

callouts.p: Always place substituted values inside brackets, especially negative numbers. For example, if x = -3, then x^2 becomes (-3)^2, which is 9, not -9.

core.p: When substituting into complex expressions, the order in which you perform calculations is critical. Errors here are the most common reason for lost marks.
A Grade 9 student must be flawless when substituting negative values into powers. This is a frequent 'distractor' in Eduqas Higher tier papers.
bullets: A negative number squared is always **positive**: (-5)^2 = 25.
A negative number cubed remains **negative**: (-2)^3 = -8.
In the expression -x^2, if x = 3, the result is -9. If x = -3, the result is -( (-3)^2 ) = -9. Note that the negative sign outside the x is applied AFTER the squaring.

fig.cap: Visual representation of why brackets are essential when squaring negative numbers to avoid sign errors.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="10" y="10" width="380" height="220" rx="15" fill="#f0f9ff" stroke="#0369a1" stroke-width="2"/><text x="50" y="50" font-family="Arial" font-size="14" fill="#0369a1" font-weight="bold">Correct Substitution: x = -4</text><rect x="40" y="70" width="140" height="60" rx="10" fill="#bbf7d0" stroke="#166534"/><text x="50" y="95" font-family="Arial" font-size="12" fill="#166534">x² = (-4) × (-4)</text><text x="50" y="115" font-family="Arial" font-size="12" fill="#166534">Result = +16</text><rect x="220" y="70" width="140" height="60" rx="10" fill="#fecaca" stroke="#991b1b"/><text x="230" y="95" font-family="Arial" font-size="12" fill="#991b1b">-x² = -(4 × 4)</text><text x="230" y="115" font-family="Arial" font-size="12" fill="#991b1b">Result = -16</text><line x1="40" y1="150" x2="360" y2="150" stroke="#0369a1" stroke-dasharray="4"/><text x="50" y="180" font-family="Arial" font-size="12" fill="#0369a1">Without brackets, -4² might be read as -(4²).</text><text x="50" y="200" font-family="Arial" font-size="12" fill="#0369a1">Always use (-4)² on your calculator!</text></svg>

core.p: Eduqas often uses 'SUVAT' equations from Physics. You must be able to substitute values into these accurately.
bullets: v = u + at (Final velocity = initial velocity + acceleration × time).
s = ut + 0.5at^2 (Displacement formula).
v^2 = u^2 + 2as (Velocity squared formula).
Be careful with **negative acceleration** (deceleration) and ensure time is squared before multiplying by 0.5a.

callouts.p: If a formula requires time in seconds but you are given minutes, convert BEFORE substituting. Formulae are unit-sensitive.

core.p: Other common scientific contexts include Kinetic Energy and Newton's Second Law.
bullets: F = ma (Force = mass × acceleration).
E = 0.5mv^2 (Kinetic Energy).
p = mv (Momentum).
In E = 0.5mv^2, only the 'v' is squared. Do not square the mass or the 0.5.

fig.cap: The structure of the Kinetic Energy formula highlighting that only the velocity is subject to the index.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="10" y="10" width="380" height="220" rx="15" fill="#fff7ed" stroke="#9a3412" stroke-width="2"/><text x="130" y="60" font-family="Arial" font-size="24" fill="#9a3412">E = ½ m v²</text><path d="M150 70 Q 150 120 100 130" fill="none" stroke="#9a3412" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/><text x="40" y="150" font-family="Arial" font-size="12" fill="#c2410c">Constant: 0.5</text><path d="M195 70 Q 195 120 200 130" fill="none" stroke="#9a3412" stroke-width="2"/><text x="180" y="150" font-family="Arial" font-size="12" fill="#c2410c">Mass (kg)</text><path d="M235 50 Q 280 50 300 100" fill="none" stroke="#9a3412" stroke-width="2"/><text x="280" y="120" font-family="Arial" font-size="12" fill="#c2410c">Only v is squared!</text><defs><marker id="arrow" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="5" refY="5" markerWidth="6" markerHeight="6" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="#9a3412"/></marker></defs></svg>

core.p: When a formula is written as a fraction, the numerator and denominator act as if they are in invisible brackets.
bullets: Calculate the entire top (numerator) first.
Calculate the entire bottom (denominator) second.
Finally, divide the numerator by the denominator.
Example: In (a + b) / c, if a=10, b=2, c=3, calculate 10+2=12 first, then 12/3=4.

core.p: A coefficient is the number in front of a variable (e.g., the 5 in 5x).
bullets: 5x means 5 multiplied by x.
5x^2 means 5 multiplied by (x squared).
Common error: Multiplying 5 by x and THEN squaring. This is wrong unless the expression is (5x)^2.

core.p: Higher tier questions may involve square roots or variables in the denominator (reciprocals).
bullets: For T = 2π√(L/g), substitute L and g first, divide them, find the square root, then multiply by 2π.
Negative results under a square root indicate a non-real solution, which usually suggests a substitution error in GCSE contexts.

core.p: Some problems require you to find one value to use in a second formula.
bullets: Step 1: Substitute into Formula A to find variable X.
Step 2: Substitute variable X into Formula B to find the final answer.
Keep full accuracy (don't round) between steps to ensure the final answer is correct to the required precision.

core.p: Quadratic expressions take the form ax^2 + bx + c. They require careful handling of signs across three terms.
bullets: Example: Evaluate 2x^2 - 5x + 3 for x = -2.
Term 3: +3.

fig.cap: Step-by-step breakdown of substituting a negative value into a quadratic expression.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="10" y="10" width="380" height="220" rx="15" fill="#f5f3ff" stroke="#5b21b6" stroke-width="2"/><text x="30" y="40" font-family="Arial" font-size="14" fill="#5b21b6" font-weight="bold">Expression: 3x² - 4x + 1 (where x = -2)</text><text x="40" y="80" font-family="Arial" font-size="12" fill="#5b21b6">Step 1 (Indices): (-2)² = 4</text><text x="40" y="110" font-family="Arial" font-size="12" fill="#5b21b6">Step 2 (Multiply): 3(4) = 12</text><text x="40" y="140" font-family="Arial" font-size="12" fill="#5b21b6">Step 3 (Middle Term): -4(-2) = +8</text><text x="40" y="170" font-family="Arial" font-size="12" fill="#5b21b6">Step 4 (Combine): 12 + 8 + 1 = 21</text><rect x="240" y="70" width="120" height="100" rx="10" fill="#ede9fe" stroke="#7c3aed"/><text x="250" y="95" font-family="Arial" font-size="11" fill="#7c3aed">Watch the signs!</text><text x="250" y="120" font-family="Arial" font-size="11" fill="#7c3aed">-4 times -2</text><text x="250" y="145" font-family="Arial" font-size="11" fill="#7c3aed">becomes +8</text></svg>

analogy.p: Think of a formula as a recipe for a cake. The variables (x, y, z) are the ingredients (flour, sugar, eggs). Substitution is the act of looking at the recipe and putting in the actual amounts specified for that day. If the recipe says '2 times the amount of sugar', and you decide to use 3 cups of sugar, you must calculate 2 x 3. The analogy breaks down because in math, the 'ingredients' can be negative or imaginary, whereas you can't have -2 eggs in a cake.

terms.d: A symbol, usually a letter, representing a quantity that can change or is unknown.
A fixed value in a formula that does not change (e.g., the number 5 or the symbol π).
A numerical or constant quantity placed before and multiplying the variable in an algebraic expression.
A mathematical phrase that can contain ordinary numbers, variables, and operators (no equals sign).
A mathematical rule expressed with symbols, usually showing the relationship between different quantities (has an equals sign).
To find the numerical value of an expression after substitution.
An acronym for the order of operations: Brackets, Indices, Division/Multiplication, Addition/Subtraction.
A number that tells you how many times to multiply a base number by itself (a power).
The size or extent of a quantity, regardless of its sign.
The result of dividing 1 by a number (e.g., the reciprocal of x is 1/x).
The top part of a fraction.
The bottom part of a fraction.

mistakes.w: Substituting x = 3 into 2x and writing 23.
mistakes.r: 2x means 2 multiplied by x, so 2(3) = 6.

mistakes.w: Calculating -5^2 as 25 on a calculator without brackets.
mistakes.r: Calculators follow BIDMAS; -5^2 is -(5^2) = -25. You must type (-5)^2 to get 25.

mistakes.w: In 3x^2, multiplying 3 by x then squaring the result.
mistakes.r: Indices come before multiplication. Square x first, then multiply by 3.

mistakes.w: Ignoring the negative sign in formulae like v = u + at when a is negative.
mistakes.r: Treat 'at' as (a) times (t). If a = -2 and t = 3, then at = -6.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to square root the final answer in v^2 = u^2 + 2as.
mistakes.r: The formula gives v squared; you must take the square root to find v.

mistakes.w: Adding terms before multiplying (e.g., 2 + 3 x 4 = 20).
mistakes.r: Multiply first: 2 + (3 x 4) = 2 + 12 = 14.

mistakes.w: Substituting values with different units (e.g., cm and m) directly.
mistakes.r: Convert all values to a consistent unit system before substituting.

exam.q: Evaluate 5a - 3b when a = 4 and b = -2.
exam.tip: Be extremely careful with the double negative (-3 times -2).

exam.q: A formula for the area of a trapezium is A = 0.5(a + b)h. Find A when a = 6, b = 10 and h = 5.
exam.tip: Work inside the brackets first.

exam.q: The kinetic energy of an object is given by E = 0.5mv^2. Calculate E when m = 10 and v = -4.
exam.tip: The square of -4 is positive 16. Energy is a scalar and cannot be negative here.

exam.q: Given y = (x^2 - 5) / (2x), find the value of y when x = -1.
exam.tip: Calculate the top and bottom separately before dividing.

exam.q: Use the formula v^2 = u^2 + 2as to find v when u = 5, a = 3 and s = 6. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
exam.tip: Don't forget the final square root step.

exam.q: Evaluate the expression 2x^3 - x^2 when x = -3.
exam.tip: A negative number cubed is negative; a negative number squared is positive.

exam.q: The period of a pendulum is T = 2π√(L/g). Find T when L = 0.98 and g = 9.8. Give your answer in terms of π.
exam.tip: Simplify the fraction inside the square root first.

exam.q: If P = I^2 R, find P when I = 0.5 and R = 200.
exam.tip: 0.5 squared is 0.25, not 1.

exam.q: The volume of a sphere is V = 4/3 π r^3. Find V when r = 3. Give your answer in terms of π.
exam.tip: 3 cubed is 27. 27 divided by 3 is 9.

worked.q: A stone is thrown upwards. Its height h after t seconds is given by h = ut - 4.9t^2. If the initial velocity u = 20 m/s, find the height of the stone after 3 seconds.
steps: Identify variables: u = 20, t = 3.
Substitute into the formula: h = (20)(3) - 4.9(3)^2.
Calculate the first term: 20 * 3 = 60.
Calculate the second term: 3^2 = 9, then 4.9 * 9 = 44.1.

worked.q: Find the value of the expression (b + sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)) / 2a when a = 2, b = 10, and c = 8.
steps: Substitute values: (10 + sqrt(10^2 - 4*2*8)) / (2*2).
Simplify inside the root: 10^2 = 100 and 4*2*8 = 64.
Subtract inside the root: 100 - 64 = 36.
Find the square root: sqrt(36) = 6.
Complete the numerator: 10 + 6 = 16.
Complete the denominator: 2 * 2 = 4.
Divide: 16 / 4 = 4.

maths_eduqas_h.1.2.summary: Algebraic vocabulary forms the structural foundation of the Eduqas GCSE Maths curriculum, requiring students to distinguish between different types of mathematical statements with absolute precision. Understanding the specific roles of expressions, equations, formulae, identities, and inequalities is crucial for interpreting exam questions correctly and applying the appropriate manipulation techniques. This topic ensures that students can identify the constituent parts of algebra—such as terms, coefficients, and factors—which is a prerequisite for higher-tier mastery of functions and proofs.

core.p: A term is a single mathematical entity that can be a number, a variable, or a product of numbers and variables. Terms are separated by addition (+) or subtraction (-) signs within a larger algebraic structure.
bullets: A **constant term** is a number on its own, such as +5 or -12.
A **variable term** contains a letter representing an unknown value, such as 3x or -y^2.
The sign (+ or -) belongs to the term that follows it.
In the expression 4x - 7, the terms are 4x and -7.

callouts.p: A number, a variable, or a combination of both multiplied together, forming a distinct part of an expression.

core.p: The coefficient is the numerical multiplier of a variable within a term. It tells us 'how many' of that variable we have. Variables are letters used to represent numbers we do not yet know or that can change.
bullets: In the term 5x, the **coefficient** is 5.
In the term -x, the **coefficient** is -1 (the 1 is often omitted but implied).
In the term x/4, the **coefficient** is 1/4.
Variables are usually written in italics in exam papers to distinguish them from units.

callouts.p: Students often mistake the coefficient of 'x' as 0. It is always 1. Similarly, the coefficient of '-x' is -1.

core.p: An expression is a collection of terms joined by operators (+, -, x, /). Crucially, an expression **does not contain an equals sign**. It represents a value but does not state that the value is equal to anything else.
bullets: Examples include 3x + 2, 5(x - 7), and (x^2 + 4)/2.
Expressions can be simplified by collecting like terms.
You cannot 'solve' an expression; you can only evaluate it if given the value of the variables.

fig.cap: Anatomy of an algebraic expression showing terms, coefficients, and constants.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="10" y="10" width="380" height="220" rx="15" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="130" y="100" font-family="Arial" font-size="40" fill="#1b2540">4x² - 7x + 5</text><line x1="145" y1="110" x2="110" y2="160" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="70" y="180" font-family="Arial" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">Coefficient (4)</text><line x1="220" y1="110" x2="220" y2="160" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="190" y="180" font-family="Arial" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">Variable (x)</text><line x1="305" y1="110" x2="340" y2="160" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="310" y="180" font-family="Arial" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">Constant (5)</text><rect x="130" y="65" width="65" height="50" fill="#dbeafe" fill-opacity="0.4" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-dasharray="4"/><text x="40" y="40" font-family="Arial" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#1b2540">Expression Components</text></svg>

core.p: An equation is a mathematical statement that two expressions are equal. It contains an equals sign (=) and is only true for **specific values** of the unknown variable.
bullets: Example: 2x + 1 = 7 is only true when x = 3.
The goal with an equation is usually to 'solve' it to find the value of the unknown.
Equations represent a balance; whatever you do to one side, you must do to the other.

callouts.p: If it has an equals sign and can be solved for a specific value, it is an equation. If it has no equals sign, it is an expression.

core.p: A formula (plural: formulae) is a special type of equation that shows the relationship between different physical quantities or variables. It usually has a single variable as the 'subject' on one side.
bullets: Example: A = πr² (Area of a circle) or F = ma (Force = mass x acceleration).
Formulae are used to calculate a value when other values are known.
Unlike a standard equation, a formula usually represents a real-world rule or geometric property.

core.p: An identity is an algebraic statement that is true for **all possible values** of the variables involved. In identities, the left-hand side is just a different way of writing the right-hand side.
bullets: Example: 2(x + 3) ≡ 2x + 6. This is true whether x is 1, 100, or -5.
The symbol ≡ (the triple bar) is used to denote an identity, meaning 'is identically equal to'.
Identities often involve expanded brackets or factorised expressions.

fig.cap: The logical difference between an Equation and an Identity.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="20" y="50" width="160" height="140" rx="10" fill="#fde68a" stroke="#1b2540"/><text x="30" y="80" font-family="Arial" font-size="14" font-weight="bold">Equation</text><text x="30" y="110" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">2x = 10</text><text x="30" y="135" font-family="Arial" font-size="11">Only true if x = 5</text><rect x="220" y="50" width="160" height="140" rx="10" fill="#bbf7d0" stroke="#1b2540"/><text x="230" y="80" font-family="Arial" font-size="14" font-weight="bold">Identity</text><text x="230" y="110" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">2(x+3) ≡ 2x+6</text><text x="230" y="135" font-family="Arial" font-size="11">True for ANY value of x</text><path d="M180 120 L220 120" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#arrow)"/><defs><marker id="arrow" markerWidth="10" markerHeight="10" refX="0" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L0,6 L9,3 z" fill="#1b2540" /></marker></defs></svg>

core.p: An inequality is a statement that compares two expressions that are not necessarily equal. It uses symbols to show which side is greater or smaller.
bullets: Symbols: < (less than), > (greater than), ≤ (less than or equal to), ≥ (greater than or equal to).
Example: x + 5 > 10. This is true for a range of values (x > 5).
Inequalities represent regions or sets of numbers rather than single points.

core.p: In algebra, factors are the expressions or numbers that are multiplied together to produce a product. Factorising is the process of breaking an expression down into these components.
bullets: In the term 6xy, the factors are 6, x, and y (and their combinations like 2, 3, 6x, etc.).
In the expression x(x + 2), the factors are x and (x + 2).
Identifying common factors is the first step in simplifying algebraic fractions.

fig.cap: Visualising factors as the dimensions of an area.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="100" y="60" width="200" height="100" fill="#e9d5ff" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="160" y1="60" x2="160" y2="160" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-dasharray="4"/><text x="120" y="115" font-family="Arial" font-size="14">x²</text><text x="210" y="115" font-family="Arial" font-size="14">5x</text><text x="175" y="50" font-family="Arial" font-size="14">x + 5</text><text x="80" y="115" font-family="Arial" font-size="14">x</text><text x="130" y="200" font-family="Arial" font-size="14" font-weight="bold">Area = x(x + 5)</text><text x="130" y="220" font-family="Arial" font-size="12">Factors are x and (x + 5)</text></svg>

analogy.p: Think of algebra as a language. A **term** is like a single word. An **expression** is like a phrase (e.g., 'the red car')—it describes something but isn't a complete thought. An **equation** is like a sentence ('The car is red')—it makes a specific claim that might be true or false. An **identity** is like a tautology ('A red car is a car that is red')—it is true by definition. This analogy breaks down because, in math, we can 'solve' sentences to find missing words, whereas in English, the words are usually fixed.

terms.d: A single number, variable, or product of both, separated by + or -.
The numerical factor of a variable term (the number in front of the letter).
A term that consists only of a number and has no variable attached.
A mathematical phrase containing terms and operators but no equals sign.
A statement that two expressions are equal, true for specific values.
A rule or relationship between different variables, often with a subject.
An equation that is true for all values of the variables.
A statement comparing two values using symbols like <, >, ≤, or ≥.
An expression or number that divides exactly into another expression.
A letter used to represent a value that can change or is unknown.
A variable in an equation for which we are trying to find a specific value.
The single variable on one side of a formula (e.g., 'A' in A = Lw).

mistakes.w: Calling 3x + 5 = 11 an expression.
mistakes.r: It is an equation because it contains an equals sign.

mistakes.w: Identifying the coefficient of -x as 0.
mistakes.r: The coefficient is -1.

mistakes.w: Thinking 2(x + 1) = 2x + 2 is an equation to be solved.
mistakes.r: It is an identity; it is true for all x, so you cannot solve it for a single value.

mistakes.w: Including the variable when asked for the coefficient (e.g., saying the coefficient of 4x is 4x).
mistakes.r: The coefficient is only the number part (4).

mistakes.w: Confusing factors with terms.
mistakes.r: Terms are added/subtracted; factors are multiplied.

mistakes.w: Using = instead of ≡ for identities in a proof.
mistakes.r: While often accepted, ≡ is the technically correct notation for identities.

mistakes.w: Saying x + y is a formula.
mistakes.r: It is an expression. A formula needs an equals sign and a subject (e.g., S = x + y).

exam.q: State whether 4x - 3 is an expression, an equation, or an identity.
exam.tip: Look for the absence of an equals sign.

exam.q: Identify the coefficient of x in the expression 7 - 5x + x^2.
exam.tip: The sign in front of the number is part of the coefficient.

exam.q: Explain why 3(x + 4) ≡ 3x + 12 is an identity.
model: It is true for all values of x.
exam.tip: Use the phrase 'true for all values' to secure the mark.

exam.q: A student writes that the terms in the expression 2x^2 - 4x + 9 are 2x^2, 4x and 9. Correct their mistake.
exam.tip: Always include the negative sign with the term.

exam.q: Which of these is a formula? A: 2x + 5 = 10, B: x(x+1), C: V = IR, D: 4x - 1 < 10.
exam.tip: Formulae usually relate different physical variables.

exam.q: Write down the three factors of the term 5xy.
exam.tip: Factors are the individual parts multiplied together.

exam.q: Is x^2 + 5x + 6 = (x + 2)(x + 3) an equation or an identity? Give a reason.
model: Because the factorised form is equal to the expanded form for every value of x.
exam.tip: If you can expand one side to get the other exactly, it is an identity.

exam.q: State the number of terms in the expression 3ab - 4a + 5b - 2.
exam.tip: Count each part separated by + or -.

exam.q: Explain the difference between an equation and an inequality.
model: An equation uses an equals sign to show two sides are the same.
An inequality uses symbols like < or > to show one side is larger or smaller than the other.
exam.tip: Focus on the symbols and the relationship they represent.

worked.q:
Classify the following four statements: 
1. 2x + 5 
2. 2x + 5 = 13 
3. A = Lw 
4. 2(x + 5) = 2x + 10
steps: Statement 1 has no equals sign, so it is an Expression.
Statement 2 has an equals sign and is only true if x = 4, so it is an Equation.
Statement 3 relates Area, Length, and Width, so it is a Formula.
Statement 4 is true for every value of x (expand the brackets to check), so it is an Identity.

worked.q:
In the expression 4x^3 - 1/2x + 7, identify: 
a) The number of terms 
b) The coefficient of x 
c) The constant term
steps: Identify the parts separated by signs: 4x^3, -1/2x, and +7. There are 3 terms.
Look at the x term: -1/2x. The number multiplying x is -1/2.
Identify the term with no variable: +7.

maths_eduqas_h.1.10.summary: Understanding the relationship between the algebraic form of a quadratic and its geometric representation is essential for Grade 9. By completing the square, we transform a standard quadratic into vertex form, which allows us to immediately identify the turning point and the line of symmetry. This algebraic manipulation is a powerful tool for sketching curves accurately and solving equations that do not easily factorise, providing a direct link between the equation's coefficients and the parabola's key features.

core.h: The Anatomy of a Quadratic Graph
core.p: A quadratic function $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ produces a U-shaped or n-shaped curve called a **parabola**. Every parabola has specific features that can be deduced algebraically.
bullets: **y-intercept**: Where the curve crosses the vertical axis (occurs when $x = 0$).
**Roots (x-intercepts)**: Where the curve crosses the horizontal axis (occurs when $y = 0$).
**Turning Point (Vertex)**: The maximum or minimum point of the curve.
**Line of Symmetry**: A vertical line passing through the turning point that divides the parabola into two mirror images.

callouts.p: The distinctive symmetrical curve formed by the graph of a quadratic function.

core.p: The y-intercept is the simplest feature to find from the general form $y = ax^2 + bx + c$.
bullets: Set $x = 0$ in the equation.
The terms $ax^2$ and $bx$ both become zero.
The remaining constant $c$ is the y-value.
The coordinate is always $(0, c)$.

fig.cap: A standard parabola showing the y-intercept at (0, c), roots on the x-axis, and the turning point at the base.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><path d="M50,40 Q200,280 350,40" fill="none" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="20" y1="180" x2="380" y2="180" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="120" y1="20" x2="120" y2="220" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="1"/><circle cx="120" stroke="#1b2540" cy="115" r="4" fill="#fecaca"/><text x="130" y="115" fill="#1b2540">y-intercept (0, c)</text><circle cx="135" cy="180" r="4" fill="#bbf7d0"/><circle cx="265" cy="180" r="4" fill="#bbf7d0"/><text x="140" y="170" fill="#1b2540">Roots</text><circle cx="200" cy="190" r="4" fill="#fde68a"/><text x="180" y="210" fill="#1b2540">Turning Point</text></svg>

core.p: To deduce the turning point, we must convert $x^2 + bx + c$ into the form $(x + p)^2 + q$. This is known as **completing the square**.
bullets: Halve the coefficient of $x$ to get $p = b/2$.
Write the bracket $(x + p)^2$.
Subtract the square of $p$ (this 'balances' the expression because $(x+p)^2$ creates an extra $p^2$ term).
Add the original constant $c$ to find $q$.

core.p: Once the equation is in the form $y = a(x + p)^2 + q$, the turning point can be read directly from the values of $p$ and $q$.
bullets: The turning point is at $(-p, q)$.
**Why?** A square $(x+p)^2$ is always $\ge 0$. The minimum value of $(x+p)^2$ is $0$, which happens when $x = -p$.
When $x = -p$, the whole expression $y = 0 + q$, so the y-coordinate is $q$.
If $a$ is positive, it is a **minimum**. If $a$ is negative, it is a **maximum**.

warn.p: Students often forget to flip the sign of the value inside the bracket. For $(x-3)^2 + 5$, the x-coordinate is +3, not -3.

core.p: If the coefficient of $x^2$ is not 1, you must factorise the $a$ out of the $x$ terms first.
bullets: Complete the square inside the square brackets: $2[(x + 3)^2 - 9] + 5$.
Expand the outer bracket: $2(x + 3)^2 - 18 + 5$.
Simplify: $2(x + 3)^2 - 13$. Turning point is $(-3, -13)$.

core.p: The roots are found by setting $y = 0$. Completing the square makes solving for $x$ straightforward without using the quadratic formula.
bullets: Rearrange: $(x + p)^2 = -q$.
Take the square root: $x + p = \pm\sqrt{-q}$.
Final roots: $x = -p \pm\sqrt{-q}$.

fig.cap: The transformation of y=x^2 to y=(x-2)^2-1. Note how the vertex moves 2 units right and 1 unit down.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><path d="M100,20 Q200,220 300,20" fill="none" stroke="#dbeafe" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="4"/><path d="M140,60 Q240,260 340,60" fill="none" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="20" y1="200" x2="380" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="200" y1="20" x2="200" y2="220" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="1"/><circle cx="200" cy="120" r="3" fill="#1b2540"/><circle cx="240" cy="160" r="4" fill="#fde68a"/><text x="165" y="110" fill="#1b2540">Original (0,0)</text><text x="250" y="175" fill="#1b2540">New (2, -1)</text></svg>

core.p: The completed square form tells us immediately how many times the curve crosses the x-axis.
Because a parabola is perfectly symmetrical, the line of symmetry always passes through the turning point.
bullets: The equation of the line of symmetry is always $x = \text{x-coordinate of turning point}$.
If the turning point is $(-p, q)$, the line of symmetry is $x = -p$.
The roots are always equidistant from this line.

core.p: The sign of the $x^2$ coefficient ($a$) determines the orientation of the turning point.
bullets: If $a > 0$, the curve is 'concave up' (smile). The turning point is a **minimum**.
If $a < 0$, the curve is 'concave down' (frown). The turning point is a **maximum**.
For a maximum, the y-value $q$ is the highest possible value the function can reach.

fig.cap: Comparison of a minimum (a > 0) and a maximum (a < 0).
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><path d="M40,40 Q100,200 160,40" fill="none" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M240,200 Q300,40 360,200" fill="none" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="60" y="220" fill="#1b2540">a is positive (Min)</text><text x="260" y="220" fill="#1b2540">a is negative (Max)</text><circle cx="100" cy="120" r="4" fill="#fde68a"/><circle cx="300" cy="120" r="4" fill="#fde68a"/></svg>

core.p: To sketch a quadratic accurately for a Grade 9 response, you must label four critical components.
bullets: 1. The **y-intercept** (found from $c$).
2. The **roots** (found by solving $y=0$).
3. The **turning point** (found by completing the square).
4. The correct **shape** (determined by the sign of $a$).

tip.p: A sketch does not need to be to scale, but the relative positions must be correct (e.g., if a root is negative, it must be to the left of the y-axis).

analogy.p: Imagine walking down into a valley. The 'Turning Point' is the exact lowest spot where you stop going down and start going up. Completing the square is like having a GPS coordinate $(-p, q)$ that tells you exactly how far across $(-p)$ and how deep $(q)$ that lowest spot is. The 'Roots' are the points where you enter and leave the valley at sea level (the x-axis). This analogy breaks down because, in real life, valleys aren't perfectly symmetrical parabolas, and they don't usually extend to infinity in both directions.

terms.d: The point where a curve changes direction from increasing to decreasing, or vice versa.
Another mathematical name for the turning point of a parabola.
A value of x for which the function f(x) = 0; where the graph hits the x-axis.
The process of writing a quadratic expression in the form a(x + p)^2 + q.
The number multiplying a variable (e.g., in 3x^2, 3 is the coefficient).
A number in an expression that does not have a variable attached.
The lowest point on a graph where a > 0.
The highest point on a graph where a < 0.
The vertical line x = k that mirrors the parabola.
A point where a graph intersects an axis.
The form y = a(x - h)^2 + k, which reveals the vertex (h, k).
An equation or function where the highest power of the variable is 2.

mistakes.w: Turning point of (x + 4)^2 - 7 is (4, -7).
mistakes.r: The turning point is (-4, -7). You must change the sign of the value inside the bracket.

mistakes.w: Completing the square for x^2 - 8x as (x - 4)^2 - 4.
mistakes.r: It should be (x - 4)^2 - 16. You must subtract the square of the half-coefficient (4 squared is 16).

mistakes.w: Saying a quadratic has no roots because it doesn't factorise.
mistakes.r: Use completing the square or the formula; many quadratics have irrational roots (surds) even if they don't factorise.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to multiply the subtracted square by 'a' when a is not 1.
mistakes.r: In 3(x+2)^2, the constant inside must be multiplied by 3 before combining with the external constant.

mistakes.w: Writing the y-intercept as just 'c' without the x=0 context.
mistakes.r: Always identify the y-intercept as the point (0, c).

mistakes.w: Confusing the line of symmetry with the y-axis.
mistakes.r: The line of symmetry is only the y-axis if the turning point has an x-coordinate of 0.

mistakes.w: Assuming all quadratics have two roots.
mistakes.r: Quadratics can have 2, 1 (repeated), or 0 real roots depending on the position of the vertex.

exam.q: Write x^2 + 10x + 3 in the form (x + a)^2 + b.
exam.tip: Always check your expansion: (x+5)(x+5) - 22 = x^2 + 10x + 25 - 22 = x^2 + 10x + 3.

exam.q: Hence, write down the coordinates of the turning point of y = x^2 + 10x + 3.
exam.tip: The word 'Hence' means you must use your previous answer.

exam.q: Find the exact roots of x^2 + 10x + 3 = 0.
exam.tip: 'Exact' usually implies leaving your answer in surd form.

exam.q: A curve has the equation y = 15 - (x - 2)^2. State the coordinates of the maximum point.
model: The equation is in vertex form: y = -1(x - 2)^2 + 15
exam.tip: The negative sign outside the bracket confirms it is a maximum (n-shape).

exam.q: Show that the quadratic x^2 + 4x + 10 has no real roots.
model: A squared number cannot be negative, so there are no real solutions.
exam.tip: In the exam, state clearly that you cannot square root a negative number for real roots.

exam.q: Express 2x^2 - 12x + 7 in the form a(x + b)^2 + c.
exam.tip: Be extremely careful with the expansion of the constant: 2 times -9 is -18.

exam.q: Write down the equation of the line of symmetry for y = 3(x + 4)^2 - 1.
exam.tip: The line of symmetry is always a vertical line 'x = ...'.

exam.q: Sketch y = x^2 - 6x + 5, showing the coordinates of the intercepts and the turning point.
model: Draw a U-shaped curve through these points.
exam.tip: Ensure the turning point is halfway between the roots (3 is halfway between 1 and 5).

exam.q: The turning point of a quadratic is (3, 7). Write its equation in the form y = x^2 + bx + c.
exam.tip: This is 'working backwards' from the turning point to the general form.

worked.q: Deduce the turning point and roots of y = x^2 - 4x - 12 by completing the square.
steps: Step 1: Complete the square. Half of -4 is -2. So, (x - 2)^2 - (-2)^2 - 12.
Step 3: Identify turning point. From (x - 2)^2 - 16, the TP is (2, -16).
Step 4: Solve for roots. Set (x - 2)^2 - 16 = 0.

worked.q: A ball is thrown. Its height h (metres) at time t (seconds) is given by h = -t^2 + 6t + 2. Find the maximum height reached.
steps: Step 1: This is a quadratic with a negative t^2, so it has a maximum.
Step 2: Complete the square. h = -[t^2 - 6t] + 2.
Step 4: Expand the bracket. h = -(t - 3)^2 + 9 + 2.
Step 6: The maximum value of h occurs when the bracket is zero.
Step 7: Max height is 11 metres (at time t = 3 seconds).

svg.cap: Visualising the 'Square' in Completing the Square: x^2 + 6x is turned into (x+3)^2 with 9 units subtracted to keep it balanced.
svg.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="50" y="50" width="100" height="100" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1b2540"/><text x="90" y="105" fill="#1b2540">x²</text><rect x="150" y="50" width="60" height="100" fill="#bbf7d0" stroke="#1b2540"/><text x="165" y="105" fill="#1b2540">3x</text><rect x="50" y="150" width="100" height="60" fill="#bbf7d0" stroke="#1b2540"/><text x="90" y="185" fill="#1b2540">3x</text><rect x="150" y="150" width="60" height="60" fill="#fecaca" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-dasharray="2"/><text x="160" y="185" fill="#1b2540">+9</text><text x="230" y="100" fill="#1b2540">Total Area = (x+3)²</text><text x="230" y="130" fill="#1b2540">Subtract 9 to get</text><text x="230" y="160" fill="#1b2540">x² + 6x</text></svg>

maths_eduqas_h.1.11.summary: Mastering the recognition and interpretation of graphs is a fundamental skill for Higher tier Eduqas GCSE Maths, bridging the gap between abstract algebra and visual geometry. Students must be able to identify the distinct 'shapes' of linear, quadratic, cubic, reciprocal, exponential, and trigonometric functions, while accurately sketching their key features such as intercepts, roots, and asymptotes. This topic requires a deep understanding of how changes in the algebraic structure of an equation directly influence the behavior and orientation of its graphical representation across the Cartesian plane, ensuring students can move fluently between equations and their visual counterparts.

core.p: Linear graphs represent a constant rate of change and always appear as straight lines. The equation is defined by two parameters: the gradient (m) and the y-intercept (c).
bullets: The gradient **m** determines the steepness; if m > 0, the line slopes upwards; if m < 0, it slopes downwards.
The y-intercept **c** is the point where the line crosses the y-axis (0, c).
Horizontal lines have the form y = k (gradient 0).
Vertical lines have the form x = k (gradient undefined).

callouts.p: Always remember: Gradient = Change in y / Change in x.

core.h: Quadratic Graphs: y = ax² + bx + c
core.p: Quadratic functions produce a symmetrical U-shaped or n-shaped curve known as a **parabola**. The shape is determined by the coefficient of x².
bullets: If **a > 0**, the graph is a 'smiley' U-shape with a minimum turning point.
If **a < 0**, the graph is a 'sad' n-shape with a maximum turning point.
The **y-intercept** is always at (0, c).
The **roots** (x-intercepts) are found where y = 0.
Every parabola has a vertical line of symmetry passing through the turning point.

core.h: Cubic Graphs: y = ax³ + bx² + cx + d
core.p: Cubic graphs generally have an 'S' shape and can have up to two turning points (a local maximum and a local minimum).
bullets: If **a > 0**, the graph starts in the bottom-left and ends in the top-right.
If **a < 0**, the graph starts in the top-left and ends in the bottom-right.
The graph can cross the x-axis at most three times (three roots).
A basic cubic like y = x³ has a 'point of inflection' at the origin rather than distinct turning points.

core.p: Reciprocal graphs are discontinuous and consist of two separate curves (hyperbolas) that never touch the axes.
bullets: The x-axis (y=0) and y-axis (x=0) are **asymptotes**.
If **k > 0**, the curves occupy the 1st and 3rd quadrants.
If **k < 0**, the curves occupy the 2nd and 4th quadrants.
As x gets very large, y gets closer to zero but never reaches it.

fig.cap: The reciprocal graph y = 1/x showing the two distinct branches and asymptotic behavior.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><line x1="200" y1="10" x2="200" y2="230" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="10" y1="120" x2="390" y2="120" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="1"/><path d="M 210 20 Q 215 115 380 118" fill="none" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M 190 220 Q 185 125 20 122" fill="none" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="280" y="40" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">y = 1/x</text><text x="210" y="20" fill="#1b2540" font-size="11">Asymptote x=0</text><text x="300" y="135" fill="#1b2540" font-size="11">Asymptote y=0</text></svg>

core.p: Similar to y = k/x, but because x is squared, the y-values have the same sign for both positive and negative x.
bullets: If **k > 0**, both branches are above the x-axis (1st and 2nd quadrants).
The graph is symmetrical about the y-axis (x = 0).
It also has asymptotes at x = 0 and y = 0.
The curve is steeper than y = 1/x near the origin.

core.p: Exponential graphs represent rapid growth or decay. The variable x is in the index (power).
bullets: If **a > 1**, the graph shows **exponential growth** (slopes upwards).
If **0 < a < 1**, the graph shows **exponential decay** (slopes downwards).
The graph **always** passes through (0, 1) because any number to the power of 0 is 1.
The negative x-axis (for growth) or positive x-axis (for decay) is a horizontal asymptote at y = 0.

fig.cap: Exponential growth graph y = 2^x, always passing through the y-intercept (0,1).
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><line x1="200" y1="20" x2="200" y2="220" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="20" y1="180" x2="380" y2="180" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="1"/><path d="M 40 178 Q 190 175 260 20" fill="none" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="200" cy="150" r="3" fill="#1b2540"/><text x="210" y="155" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">(0, 1) intercept</text><text x="280" y="60" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">y = a^x</text><text x="40" y="200" fill="#1b2540" font-size="11">Approaches y=0</text></svg>

core.p: The graph of y = sin x is a periodic wave that repeats every 360 degrees.
bullets: The maximum value is 1 (at 90°) and the minimum value is -1 (at 270°).
It passes through the origin (0, 0).
Roots (x-intercepts) occur at 0°, 180°, and 360°.
The **amplitude** is 1 and the **period** is 360°.

core.p: The graph of y = cos x is the same shape as the sine graph but translated (shifted) 90° to the left.
bullets: The maximum value is 1 (at 0° and 360°) and the minimum is -1 (at 180°).
It passes through (0, 1) on the y-axis.
Roots (x-intercepts) occur at 90° and 270°.
Like sine, it has an amplitude of 1 and a period of 360°.

fig.cap: One full cycle of the Sine and Cosine waves from 0 to 360 degrees.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><line x1="40" y1="120" x2="360" y2="120" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="40" y1="20" x2="40" y2="220" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="1"/><path d="M 40 120 Q 120 20 200 120 T 360 120" fill="none" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="4"/><path d="M 40 20 Q 120 20 120 120 T 280 220 T 360 120" fill="none" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="50" y="140" fill="#1b2540" font-size="11">0</text><text x="190" y="140" fill="#1b2540" font-size="11">180</text><text x="340" y="140" fill="#1b2540" font-size="11">360</text><text x="260" y="40" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">Dashed: Sine</text><text x="260" y="60" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">Solid: Cosine</text></svg>

core.p: The graph of y = tan x is very different from sine and cosine; it is not a continuous wave.
bullets: It has vertical **asymptotes** at 90°, 270°, and every 180° thereafter.
The period is 180° (it repeats more frequently than sine/cosine).
The value of tan x goes to infinity as it approaches the asymptotes.
It passes through the origin (0, 0) and has roots at 0°, 180°, and 360°.

callouts.p: Calculators will show an error for tan(90) because the graph never reaches a value there; it is undefined.

core.p: Interpreting a graph involves identifying specific points that solve algebraic equations.
bullets: **Roots** of f(x) = 0 are the x-coordinates where the graph crosses the x-axis.
The **y-intercept** is the value of the function when x = 0.
**Intersection points** of two graphs y = f(x) and y = g(x) are the solutions to the equation f(x) = g(x).
**Turning points** indicate the maximum or minimum value of a function within a range.

analogy.p: Think of equations as 'DNA' and graphs as the 'Faces' they produce. Just as you can recognize a person by their silhouette, you can recognize a quadratic by its U-shape or a reciprocal by its split branches. A linear graph is like a straight path, while a trig graph is like the repetitive motion of a pendulum. The analogy breaks down because while human faces change over time, a mathematical function's graph is eternally fixed by its equation; if the DNA (equation) stays the same, the Face (graph) can never change.

terms.d: A line that a graph approaches increasingly closely but never actually touches or crosses.
The specific U-shaped curve representing a quadratic function.
The horizontal distance after which a periodic function (like sine or cosine) repeats its pattern.
The maximum displacement of a wave from its central equilibrium position.
The x-values where a graph intersects the x-axis (where y = 0).
A point on a curve where the gradient changes from positive to negative (maximum) or vice versa (minimum).
A function of the form y = k/x, where the variable is in the denominator.
A function where the variable is the exponent, such as y = a^x.
The point where a graph crosses an axis.
A geometric property where one part of the graph is a reflection of another.
A graph that can be drawn without lifting the pen from the paper (unlike tan x or 1/x).
A measure of the steepness of a line or curve at a specific point.

mistakes.w: Drawing a reciprocal graph (y=1/x) so that it touches the x or y axes.
mistakes.r: The curves must approach the axes but never touch them, as they are asymptotes.

mistakes.w: Starting the cosine graph at the origin (0,0).
mistakes.r: The cosine graph starts at (0,1). The sine graph starts at (0,0).

mistakes.w: Drawing an exponential graph (y=2^x) passing through (0,0).
mistakes.r: Any number to the power of 0 is 1, so it must pass through (0,1).

mistakes.w: Sketching a cubic graph as a straight line or a simple parabola.
mistakes.r: A cubic must show the characteristic 'S' curve or turning points.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to draw the second branch of a reciprocal graph in the third quadrant.
mistakes.r: Reciprocal graphs (y=1/x) have two parts; you must show both.

mistakes.w: Drawing the tangent graph as a continuous wave like sine.
mistakes.r: The tangent graph must have clear breaks (asymptotes) at 90 and 270 degrees.

mistakes.w: Confusing y = 1/x with y = 1/x².
mistakes.r: y = 1/x² is always positive (above the x-axis), whereas y = 1/x has a negative branch.

exam.q: Sketch the graph of y = sin x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360.
exam.tip: Use a pencil and draw a smooth curve; avoid 'pointy' peaks.

exam.q: Identify the type of graph represented by the equation y = 3^x.
exam.tip: If x is the power, it is always exponential.

exam.q: State the coordinates of the y-intercept for the graph y = x² - 5x + 6.
exam.tip: The y-intercept is always the constant term 'c'.

exam.q: Sketch the graph of y = 1/x.
model: Two curves drawn in the 1st and 3rd quadrants.
Curves approach but do not touch the x and y axes.
exam.tip: Ensure the branches look symmetrical.

exam.q: A graph has asymptotes at x = 90 and x = 270. Which trigonometric function is this?
exam.tip: Only the tangent function has vertical asymptotes in the standard GCSE range.

exam.q: Sketch y = -x³.
model: Cubic shape passing through the origin.
Graph goes from top-left to bottom-right (negative coefficient).
exam.tip: A negative x³ is a reflection of y = x³ in the x-axis.

exam.q: Explain why the graph of y = 2^x never crosses the x-axis.
model: As x becomes more negative, 2^x becomes a smaller and smaller fraction.
However, 2^x will always be greater than zero, so it never reaches the axis.
exam.tip: This is the definition of a horizontal asymptote.

exam.q: On the same axes, sketch y = x² and y = x² + 3.
model: y = x² + 3 is clearly shifted upwards.
exam.tip: The '+3' is a vertical translation.

exam.q: Find the roots of the graph y = x(x - 4).
exam.tip: Roots are where the graph hits the x-axis.

worked.q: Sketch the graph of y = cos x for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°, labelling all intercepts with the axes.
steps: Identify the y-intercept: cos(0) = 1, so the graph starts at (0, 1).
Identify the x-intercepts (roots): cos(x) = 0 at 90° and 270°.
Identify the minimum point: cos(180) = -1, so the turning point is (180, -1).
Identify the end point: cos(360) = 1, so the graph ends at (360, 1).
Draw a smooth wave connecting these points.
worked.ans: A smooth 'bucket' shaped wave starting at (0,1), crossing x at 90 and 270, with a minimum at (180,-1).

worked.q: Match the following equations to their shapes: A) y = 4/x, B) y = x³ - x, C) y = 0.5^x.
steps: Equation A is a reciprocal (k/x), so it will be two branches in quadrants 1 and 3.
Equation B is a cubic (x³), so it will be an S-shape crossing the x-axis up to 3 times.
Equation C is an exponential with a base between 0 and 1 (0.5), so it will be an exponential decay curve.
worked.ans: A: Reciprocal, B: Cubic, C: Exponential Decay.

svg.cap: Standard Cubic Graph y = x³ showing the point of inflection at the origin.
svg.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><line x1="200" y1="10" x2="200" y2="230" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="10" y1="120" x2="390" y2="120" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="1"/><path d="M 100 220 C 150 220 180 120 200 120 C 220 120 250 20 300 20" fill="none" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="280" y="50" fill="#1b2540" font-size="12">y = x³</text><text x="160" y="110" fill="#1b2540" font-size="11">Inflection (0,0)</text></svg>

maths_eduqas_h.1.17.summary: Quadratic equations represent relationships where the highest power of the variable is two, creating a characteristic U-shaped curve known as a parabola. Solving these equations means finding the 'roots' or 'zeros'—the specific x-values that make the equation equal to zero. This can be done through factorising for simple cases, completing the square to find turning points, or using the quadratic formula for any equation, while graphical methods provide visual approximations by identifying where the curve crosses the x-axis.

core.p: Before applying any algebraic method, a quadratic equation must be rearranged into its **standard form**. This ensures all coefficients are correctly identified for the formula or factorising process.
bullets: The standard form is ax^2 + bx + c = 0.
a is the coefficient of x^2, b is the coefficient of x, and c is the constant term.
If the equation is not equal to zero, move terms across the equals sign by performing inverse operations.
Ensure 'a' is positive where possible to make factorising easier.

callouts.p: You cannot solve a quadratic by factorising if the other side of the equation isn't zero. For example, if x^2 + 5x = -6, you must add 6 to both sides first.

core.p: When the coefficient of x^2 is 1, we look for two numbers that satisfy two specific conditions simultaneously.
bullets: Find two numbers that **multiply** to give 'c' (the constant).
The same two numbers must **add** to give 'b' (the coefficient of x).
Write the factors in the form (x + p)(x + q) = 0.
Example: x^2 + 5x + 6 = 0. Numbers 2 and 3 work because 2*3=6 and 2+3=5. Factorised: (x+2)(x+3)=0.

core.p: This is the logical step that allows us to find the actual solutions once the expression is factorised.
bullets: If the product of two brackets is zero, at least one of the brackets must be zero.
Set each bracket equal to zero: x + p = 0 or x + q = 0.
Solve these simple linear equations to find the roots.
For (x+2)(x+3)=0, the solutions are x = -2 and x = -3.

callouts.p: Notice that the sign of the solution is usually the opposite of the sign inside the bracket.

core.p: When 'a' is not 1, we use the 'ac' method (splitting the middle term).
bullets: Multiply 'a' and 'c' together.
Find two numbers that multiply to 'ac' and add to 'b'.
Split the 'bx' term into two parts using these numbers.
Factorise the first two terms and the last two terms separately (factorising by grouping).
Example: 2x^2 + 7x + 3. ac = 6. Numbers 6 and 1 work. 2x^2 + 6x + x + 3 = 2x(x+3) + 1(x+3) = (2x+1)(x+3).

core.p: This method transforms the quadratic into a form where 'x' only appears once, making it solvable by rearranging.
bullets: The form is (x + p)^2 + q = 0.
The value of 'p' is always half of 'b'.
Subtract the square of 'p' to maintain equality.

fig.cap: Visualising Completing the Square: We take the 'bx' rectangle, split it in half, and move one part to the side. The 'missing corner' is (b/2)^2.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="50" y="50" width="100" height="100" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1b2540"/><rect x="150" y="50" width="60" height="100" fill="#fde68a" stroke="#1b2540"/><rect x="50" y="150" width="100" height="60" fill="#fde68a" stroke="#1b2540"/><rect x="150" y="150" width="60" height="60" fill="#fecaca" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-dasharray="4"/><text x="90" y="105" font-size="12">x^2</text><text x="165" y="105" font-size="12">bx/2</text><text x="80" y="185" font-size="12">bx/2</text><text x="155" y="185" font-size="11">Missing</text><text x="155" y="200" font-size="11">(b/2)^2</text></svg>

core.p: Once the square is completed, we isolate the squared bracket and take the square root.
bullets: Move the constant 'q' to the other side.
Take the square root of both sides, remembering the plus or minus sign.
Subtract 'p' to find the final values of x.

core.p: This is the fail-safe method that works for any quadratic equation, especially when roots are irrational (decimals or surds).
bullets: Formula: x = [-b ± sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)] / 2a.
Substitute values carefully, using brackets for negative numbers.
Calculate the value under the square root (the discriminant) first.
Simplify the fraction to find two solutions.

fig.cap: The Quadratic Formula components: The discriminant determines the number of real solutions.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="20" y="60" width="360" height="120" rx="10" fill="#e9d5ff" stroke="#1b2540"/><text x="60" y="110" font-size="24" font-family="serif">x = </text><line x1="100" y1="105" x2="340" y2="105" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="110" y="95" font-size="18">-b ± √(b² - 4ac)</text><text x="200" y="130" font-size="18">2a</text><text x="210" y="160" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">Discriminant: b² - 4ac</text></svg>

core.h: The Discriminant and Nature of Roots
core.p: The expression b^2 - 4ac tells us how many solutions exist without solving the whole equation.
Graphs provide a visual way to solve equations by looking for specific intersection points.
bullets: To solve ax^2 + bx + c = 0, look for the x-intercepts (where y = 0).
To solve ax^2 + bx + c = k, look for where the curve intersects the horizontal line y = k.
Read the x-coordinates of these points as accurately as possible.
If the curve is between grid lines, estimate to one decimal place.

fig.cap: Solving x^2 - 4x + 3 = 0 graphically. The roots are the x-values where the curve crosses the x-axis (y=0).
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><line x1="50" y1="180" x2="350" y2="180" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="80" y1="20" x2="80" y2="220" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M 100,40 Q 200,320 300,40" fill="none" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="135" y="180" r="4" fill="#fecaca"/><circle cx="265" y="180" r="4" fill="#fecaca"/><text x="110" y="170" font-size="12">Root 1</text><text x="250" y="170" font-size="12">Root 2</text><text x="360" y="185" font-size="12">x</text><text x="70" y="30" font-size="12">y</text></svg>

core.h: Solving Equations of the form f(x) = g(x)
core.p: Sometimes you are asked to solve a quadratic by finding the intersection with a linear graph.
bullets: Example: Solve x^2 - 5x + 2 = x - 3.
Plot y = x^2 - 5x + 2 and y = x - 3 on the same axes.
The x-coordinates of the points where they cross are the solutions.
Algebraically, this is the same as solving x^2 - 6x + 5 = 0.

core.p: Efficiency is key in exams. Choosing the right tool saves time and reduces errors.
bullets: **Factorising:** Use first if the numbers look 'friendly' (small integers).
**Formula:** Use if factorising isn't obvious or if the question asks for decimal places/surds.
**Completing the Square:** Use if the question specifically asks for it, or to find the turning point (vertex).
**Graphs:** Use when a sketch is provided or when an 'estimate' is requested.

core.p: Complex quadratics may require algebraic simplification before they can be solved.
bullets: If the equation has fractions, multiply every term by the common denominator to clear them.
If there are brackets, expand them first and collect like terms.
Always aim for the ax^2 + bx + c = 0 structure before starting your chosen method.

analogy.p: Solving a quadratic is like trying to open a locked door. Factorising is like using a specific key; it's the fastest way, but it only works if the key fits the lock (if the numbers are integers). Completing the square is like using a adjustable wrench; it takes a bit more effort to set up, but it can handle many different sizes. The Quadratic Formula is like a heavy-duty battering ram; it's bulky and takes time to assemble, but it is guaranteed to open any door, no matter how tough the lock is. The analogy breaks down because, in maths, the 'battering ram' (formula) is actually derived from the 'wrench' (completing the square), showing they are fundamentally the same logic.

terms.d: An equation where the highest power of the unknown variable is 2.
A value of x that satisfies the equation (makes it equal to zero).
The number multiplying a variable (e.g., in 3x^2, 3 is the coefficient).
A term in an algebraic expression that has a fixed value and no variable.
The part of the quadratic formula (b^2 - 4ac) that determines the nature of the roots.
The name of the U-shaped curve produced by a quadratic function.
A quadratic where the coefficient of x^2 is exactly 1.
To write an expression as a product of its factors (usually in brackets).
The turning point of a parabola (the maximum or minimum point).
The principle that if ab = 0, then a = 0 or b = 0.
An irrational number expressed as a root (e.g., √5).
The arrangement ax^2 + bx + c = 0.
The point where a graph crosses an axis.
The process of removing brackets by multiplying terms.

mistakes.w: x^2 = 16 therefore x = 4
mistakes.r: x = ±4 (always include the negative root).

mistakes.w: Using the formula with -b as -5 when b is -5.

mistakes.r: The equation must equal zero before factorising.

mistakes.w: Dividing the whole equation by x to solve x^2 + 5x = 0.
mistakes.r: Factorise out the x: x(x+5)=0. Dividing by x loses the solution x=0.

mistakes.w: In the formula, only putting the square root over 2a.
mistakes.r: The entire numerator (-b ± √...) must be divided by 2a.

mistakes.w: When completing the square for x^2 - 8x, writing (x - 4)^2 + 16.
mistakes.r: It should be (x - 4)^2 - 16. You always subtract the square.

mistakes.w: Thinking 'no real roots' means 'no solutions at all'.
mistakes.r: It means the graph doesn't cross the x-axis; solutions exist in complex numbers, but not for GCSE.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to multiply 'a' and 'c' when factorising 2x^2 + 7x + 3.
mistakes.r: You must find numbers that multiply to 6 (2*3), not just 3.

exam.q: Solve x^2 - 8x + 15 = 0 by factorising.
exam.tip: Check your signs: -3 * -5 = +15 and -3 + -5 = -8.

model: 3 * -10 = -30. Factors of -30 that add to 13 are 15 and -2.
exam.tip: Always check if the quadratic can be factorised before jumping to the formula.

exam.q: Solve x^2 + 10x - 3 = 0 by completing the square. Leave your answer in surd form.
exam.tip: Eduqas often asks for 'exact form' or 'surd form'—this is a hint to complete the square.

exam.q: Use the quadratic formula to solve 2x^2 - 7x - 1 = 0. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.
exam.tip: Be extremely careful with the -4ac part when c is negative; it becomes a plus.

exam.q: A curve has the equation y = x^2 + x - 5. Use the graph to estimate the solutions to x^2 + x - 5 = 0.
model: Identify where the curve crosses the x-axis.
exam.tip: Draw a clear dot on the x-axis where the line crosses to show the examiner your method.

exam.q: Show that the equation x^2 + 4x + 7 = 0 has no real solutions.
model: Since the discriminant is negative, there are no real solutions.
exam.tip: You must state the conclusion clearly to get the final mark.
Don't expand the brackets! It's already in a form where you can just square root.

exam.q: Rearrange and solve: x + 4 = 12/x
exam.tip: Multiplying by x is a common first step for equations with x in the denominator.

exam.q: Solve 5x^2 - 20 = 0.
exam.tip: If there is no 'bx' term, you can solve by simple isolation and square rooting.

exam.q: The diagram shows the graph of y = x^2 - 3x. Use the graph to solve x^2 - 3x = 2.
model: Draw the horizontal line y = 2 on the graph.
Find the x-coordinates of the intersection points.
exam.tip: The line y=2 must be straight and drawn with a ruler.

worked.q: Solve the equation 6x^2 - 11x - 10 = 0 by factorising.
steps: Multiply a and c: 6 * -10 = -60.
Find factors of -60 that add to -11: -15 and 4.
Split the middle term: 6x^2 - 15x + 4x - 10 = 0.
Factorise in pairs: 3x(2x - 5) + 2(2x - 5) = 0.

worked.q: Solve x^2 - 6x + 2 = 0 by completing the square, giving your answer in the form a ± √b.
steps: Half of -6 is -3, so start with (x - 3)^2.
Expand (x - 3)^2 to get x^2 - 6x + 9.
We need +2, so subtract 7: (x - 3)^2 - 7 = 0.
Isolate the square: (x - 3)^2 = 7.
Square root: x - 3 = ±√7.
